title: Who's asking?
author: Chris Reid
summary: Chris Reid draws on his own teaching and doctoral research to ask what questions students actually ask and who asks them. He sorts everyday classroom questions into confusion, distraction and evasion questions, and contrasts them with genuine curiosity questions. He cites Andrew Whittaker's observation study, which found that students sometimes ask too many inquiry questions and derail a lesson. Using the SSES and PISA 2022 data, he shows that 15-year-olds are about as curious as 10-year-olds but less likely to say they like asking questions. The willingness to ask varies far more by family wealth and maths attainment than by gender, and East Asian systems score lowest. He concludes that curiosity is celebrated in policy documents while classrooms reward compliance and recall, which raises the question of what schools are for.
points: Reid separates student questions into confusion, distraction and evasion types, and notes that most of them are not curiosity at all.
Whittaker's small study suggests that students can ask too many inquiry questions, which makes curiosity a real threat to a teacher's planned lesson.
International survey data show curiosity holds steady between ages 10 and 15 while the stated liking for asking questions falls from 64% to 55%.
The gaps in who likes asking questions are larger by wealth and attainment than by gender, in nearly every country group.
Reid argues that schools reward compliance and accurate recall, so curiosity gets hidden behind performances students use to survive secondary school.
quotes: Confusion questions aren’t really questions at all. Usually, a kid will put up their hand (if I’m lucky) and tell me they just don’t get it.
It’s hard to tell, as a teacher, whether a student really wants to know the answer, or simply wants to signal something to their classmates, like their boredom – or to take the lesson off course.
He concluded that, rather than students asking too few questions, ‘they may, in some circumstances, ask too many’.
In every bloc, though, the gender gap is much lower than the gaps by wealth and attainment.

Instead of completely disappearing, maybe curiosity is hidden behind these performances that allow students to survive in the secondary classroom, to navigate the unwritten rules, the norms, and expectations from teachers and classmates alike.
Curiosity is more often celebrated rhetorically, in policy documents and departmental mission statements than it is in the classroom. There, we often celebrate compliance and accurate recall.
